overview: Multan here is one enduring city-region, not one immortal state. The atlas supplies two records separated by 783 years: a tenth-century amirate and Fatimid-aligned principality from 900 to 1000, then a Durrani province under Muzaffar Khan from 1783 to 1800. The summaries are identical, but their governments differed. The map geometry is even stranger: its 900 “Multan” polygon misses Multan city and reaches south around Bahawalpur; its 1783 polygon includes the city but blankets much of southwest Punjab. Neither is a surveyed frontier. Medieval Multan prospered through pilgrimage, farming, caravans, and silver coinage. Tiny dammas combined Indic and Arabic writing before Fatimid-style coins advertised a new allegiance. Mosques, the Sun Temple, merchants, artisans, and competing Muslim traditions shared an unequal urban landscape. Centuries later, Muzaffar Khan governed amid Durrani claims, Sikh pressure, forts, bazaars, shrines, Persian letters, and travelling performers. A rare manuscript lets Murad Bakhsh ride, sing, bargain, parent, and resist elite control. The atlas ends both phases early: Mahmud’s attacks came after 1000, while Muzaffar ruled until the Sikh conquest of 1818. The city continued through every recoloring.

periods.title: 712 to 850: conquest, temple revenue, and a frontier city
periods.summary: Arab armies took Multan in the early eighth century, but conquest did not erase the older sacred and commercial landscape. The Sun Temple remained a pilgrimage center, while administrators linked the city to Sind. Later writers describe treasure and revenue; their dramatic numbers should be read as political storytelling, not audited accounts.

periods.title: 850 to 958: locally rooted amirs and bilingual money
periods.summary: A locally established Qurashi family, often called Banu Samah or Banu Munabbih, asserted autonomy. Its tiny silver dammas joined regional Indic titles and symbols with Kufic Arabic. Coin evidence shows rulers speaking to several political and religious audiences at once, while exact reign lists and dates remain debated.

periods.title: 958 to 1005: Fatimid allegiance in the atlas interval
periods.summary: An Ismaili principality emerged in the later tenth century and acknowledged the Fatimid imam-caliph rather than the Abbasid caliph. Al-Muqaddasi encountered a prosperous city in 985. Its foundation date and the Sun Temple’s destruction remain disputed; Multan’s al-Aziz coins securely date Fatimid-style minting to 975 to 996.

periods.title: 1005 to 1175: Ghaznavid attacks and changing overlords
periods.summary: Mahmud of Ghazni attacked in 1005, imposed tribute, returned, and violently targeted Ismaili power. This ended the independent Fatimid-aligned principality, not Multan as a city. Governors, worshippers, traders, and households persisted under changing regimes, although court narratives illuminate conquest far better than ordinary recovery.

periods.title: 1175 to 1398: frontier administration and a shrine city
periods.summary: Ghurid and Delhi-based rulers made Multan a western frontier. Suhrawardi teachers, patrons, builders, and pilgrims reshaped its sacred geography. Bahauddin Zakariya settled there in the early thirteenth century; the monumental tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam followed from 1320 to 1324, combining brick, timber, and glazed decoration.

periods.title: 1398 to 1526: invasion, recovery, and Langah rule
periods.summary: Timur’s invasion damaged the region, after which Multan passed through contested governors and an independent Langah sultanate. Agricultural and caravan routes again supported prosperity. The period demonstrates why a place-history card needs several governments: “Multan” can name a city, province, dynasty, or commercial zone without making them identical.

periods.title: 1526 to 1739: Mughal provincial capital and mint
periods.summary: Mughal rulers incorporated Multan as a major province and mint. Riverine cultivation, textile production, overland trade, mosques, shrines, and specialized bazaars supported the city. Administrative reach changed by reign, so the broad provincial name should not be mistaken for one fixed boundary around today’s district.

periods.title: 1739 to 1779: Mughal collapse, Durrani claims, and Sikh occupation
periods.summary: After Nadir Shah and Mughal decline, Ahmad Shah Durrani claimed Multan. Bhangi Sikh forces occupied the city from 1772 to 1779 and minted there. Timur Shah recovered the citadel in 1779. These quick transfers explain the unstable setting inherited by Muzaffar Khan and refute a tidy uninterrupted Durrani block.

periods.title: 1779 to 1800: Muzaffar Khan’s Durrani-era Multan
periods.summary: Muzaffar Khan governed Multan within a Durrani political world but exercised substantial local power. He founded fortified Muzaffargarh in 1794. Persian manuscript culture, travelling performers, messengers, elite households, shrines, farms, markets, and military demands reveal a regional society richer than the atlas’s single colored polygon.

periods.title: 1800 to 1818: atlas removal before the actual conquest
periods.summary: The atlas recolors Multan as Sikh in 1800 and then Maratha in 1815. Muzaffar Khan nevertheless remained ruler until Ranjit Singh’s army captured the fort in 1818. The conquest ended his regime amid death and plunder; it did not end the city, its families, markets, shrines, crafts, or languages.

sections.title: Two map cards, one city, not one state

items.text: The index contains two exact missing records named Multan: 900 to 1000 and 1783 to 1800. Their imported summaries are byte-identical modern-city prose. Sharing one card avoids duplicate place history, but the 783-year gap is structural: these are a medieval amirate and a Durrani-era province, never one uninterrupted dynasty.

The 900 polygon fails the most basic place test. Its latitude stops near 29.62 degrees north, below Multan at roughly 30.2; of seventeen fixed probes, it contains only Bahawalpur. At that same snapshot the actual Multan probes belong to the atlas’s Samanid Empire feature. The label and shape plainly disagree.

The 1783 polygon does contain Multan, its fort, and nearby river corridor, but it also contains Muzaffargarh, Uch, Bahawalpur, Dera Ghazi Khan, Jhang, Dipalpur, and Dera Ismail Khan. Seven polygon positions cannot document every local jurisdiction inside that enormous envelope. It is a coarse atlas tile.

All fifty tracked border snapshots were audited. Each target appears exactly once, in one snapshot and one feature, with no duplicate, mixed, or out-of-lifetime geometry. The database is internally tidy while historically misleading: consistency proves where the software put a shape, not whether the shape belongs there.

Direct shared arcs make the problem visible. The 900 feature touches Sindh, Chauhans, Hindu Shahis, Gurjara-Pratihara, Samanids, and Saffarids in the imported tiling. The 1783 feature touches Afghanistan, Sind, Lahore, and “Mahratta States.” These are polygon neighbors, not proof of treaties, wars, languages, or ethnic borders.

sections.title: Merchants, pilgrims, temples, and mosques around 900 to 1000

items.text: Peer-reviewed research calls tenth-century Multan a mercantile cosmopolis at the edge of larger Muslim empires. Its rulers depended on traders and pilgrims and could not simply copy politics from Baghdad or Cairo. Religious variety was practical reality as well as belief, and tolerance remained unequal, contingent, and vulnerable to regime change.

The Sun Temple drew pilgrims and offerings long after the eighth-century conquest. Al-Muqaddasi still described it in 985, so claims that it certainly vanished in 965 run into contemporary geographic evidence. Its final destruction belongs to a contested sequence around the Fatimid transition and Ghaznavid attacks, not a clean textbook timestamp.

DAMAST links Multan’s mosque, temple, Shi‘i population, and other religious evidence directly to al-Muqaddasi and modern scholarship, with confidence ratings rather than pretending every statement is equally certain. The city’s sacred landscape included rival institutions close to markets; coexistence does not mean equal rights or permanent harmony.

The Fatimid-aligned rulers had the khutba proclaimed for Cairo’s imam-caliph, making Friday worship a public statement of sovereignty. That political allegiance did not turn all residents into Ismailis. The city still included other Muslims and non-Muslim communities, while sources largely preserve arguments among male elites rather than household belief.

Merchants moved through Multan between the Indus plains, Afghanistan, Iran, and Central Asia. Coins, pilgrims, and geographic accounts confirm connectivity without giving us a complete customs ledger. A caravan hub could be cosmopolitan and dangerous at once: roads carried silver, cloth, stories, teachers, taxes, disease, soldiers, and very tired animals.

sections.title: Tiny coins speak in two scripts

items.text: A silver damma of Munabbih in the British Museum is only ten millimetres wide and weighs half a gram. It combines a two-line Nagari inscription with a three-dot motif, Nagari characters, and Kufic Arabic. Medieval wallets apparently expected excellent eyesight, or at least fingers good at recognizing very small money.

Written-language sample for the early era, in scholarly transliteration: “Śrī Bharatha” on the proto-Sharada side, and “li-llāh Sulaymān,” meaning “for Allah, [issued by] Sulayman,” in Kufic Arabic. The ninth- or tenth-century dammas are bilingual objects; their period letterforms survive in photographs, so modern fonts are not substituted as facsimiles.

The same coin study identifies Indic royal titles such as Śrī Ādi Varāha alongside an amir’s Arabic name. That was political communication across communities, not evidence that ruler and every user shared one blended faith. Money travels by trust: familiar titles and symbols can help a new authority sound locally legible.

A later British Museum coin securely minted at Multan between 975 and 996 names the Fatimid caliph al-‘Aziz and carries four lines of Kufic on each side. At eight millimetres and 0.55 grammes, it makes a major international allegiance fit onto something smaller than a child’s fingernail.

Coins survive selectively. Hoards favor metal over cloth receipts, wooden tallies, spoken bargains, and debts settled without minting anything. Curatorial research has expanded the known Arab Sind and Multan corpus, but it cannot reveal the purse of every farmer, potter, pilgrim, woman, child, servant, or enslaved person.

sections.title: Streets, walls, farms, bazaars, and work

items.text: Al-Muqaddasi’s Arabic geography is unusually attentive to cities, markets, buildings, water, and social reputation. It is still one educated male traveller’s arranged account, not a census. His observations help reconstruct late tenth-century Multan only when translations, editions, genre, and the temptation to turn vivid description into universal daily life are kept visible.

The digitized Arabic edition lets readers inspect the source behind later summaries rather than recycling a quotation of a quotation. It does not provide a street-by-street archaeological plan. Small houses, heat, trade, and cleanliness judgments in geographic literature must remain observations shaped by comparison, rhetoric, route, and the visitor’s access.

Multan’s wider plain sits among Indus tributaries, with agriculture depending on rivers, seasonal channels, wells, labor, and political control of revenue. The city’s trading role rested on food and raw materials produced beyond its walls. Court and travel texts rarely name the cultivators who made urban prosperity edible.

A study of the old city describes a citadel mound separated from a densely enclosed settlement, with a broad approach feeding Chowk Bazaar and narrower specialized markets branching toward gates. Its surviving layout is not frozen tenth-century evidence, but it explains how walls, shops, worship, movement, and congestion accumulated over many eras.

The same urban record places a 1757 mosque beside shops and notes bazaars for general goods, clothing, perfumes, and specialized trades. That gives a grounded late-eighteenth-century setting: worship and business met at street scale. It does not tell us each shopkeeper’s religion, rent, family arrangement, profit, or toilet location.

sections.title: Families, women, children, and unequal power

items.text: The 1806 to 1807 Persian Jaur-o-Jafa sets much of its story in the reign of Timur Shah and names Muzaffar Khan. It follows the Multani courtesan Murad Bakhsh, yet its male narrator is defensive and hostile. The manuscript offers rare social detail only when Murad’s choices are separated from his accusations.

Murad travelled with musicians, dancers, servants, horses, and sometimes camels, seeking patronage beyond Multan. She was an employer and skilled performer, not merely an ornament in a nobleman’s story. Her mobility also exposed her to elite surveillance, legal coercion, financial dependence, and threatened violence.

Murad’s wish to visit her children shows professional performers also carried family responsibilities. The record does not name each child, age, caregiver, home routine, or education. That absence matters: a woman can be a parent, wage earner, artist, traveller, and legal actor even when a male text prefers a romance plot.

Elite households used kinship, servants, messengers, patronage, and hereditary rank to move resources and settle disputes. The manuscript also shows that “family” could include obligations across cities. It says far less about farmers’ households, craft apprentices, widows outside elite circles, or how ordinary children divided play, chores, and learning.

Muzaffar Khan founded fortified Muzaffargarh in 1794 across the Chenab-side region. A governor’s new town required builders, transporters, soldiers, traders, cultivators, and families, although the official history preserves the founder more clearly than the workforce. Cities do not spring fully built from a nawab’s extremely confident pointing finger.

The tenth-century city used Arabic in administration and religious life while Indic scripts remained on local money; Persian was also part of the wider region’s learned and commercial world. Bilingual coins prove planned written communication. They do not prove universal literacy, identical pronunciation, or that every child attended a formal school.

No reviewed source securely describes a tenth-century Multan classroom, enrollment list, girls’ school, slate, lesson timetable, or teacher’s pay. Mosques, temples, merchants, coin engravers, and officials required learned specialists, yet specialist literacy cannot be turned into mass schooling. Someone learned the scripts; we do not know who got a desk.

Written-language sample for the late era: Persian “ضرب ملتان” (zarb Multān), meaning “struck at Multan,” is the mint formula catalogued on regional coins. Persian served official and literary communication, while Punjabi and Saraiki speech continued beyond the written archive. A mint label records authority, not everyone’s home language.

Jaur-o-Jafa survives in Persian nasta‘liq, continuous prose, and more than two hundred quoted verses, with paintings of performance and travel. Its mixed prose and poetry required scribes, readers, musicians, and memory. The quoted poems sometimes differ from standard editions, evidence of living oral performance rather than sloppy ancient copy-paste.

A munshi, messengers, written promises, letters, and literary gatherings appear in the late-eighteenth-century world. Murad demanded written assurance for her safety, showing writing could become practical protection as well as art. It did not guarantee justice: a document still depended on people powerful enough, or shamed enough, to honor it.

sections.title: Food, water, medicine, sanitation, and toilets

items.text: The rivers and channels around Multan supported fields, orchards, transport, and settlement while also bringing floods and shifting courses. Urban-growth research remembers an old riverbed beside the citadel. It does not supply a tenth- or eighteenth-century municipal water map, household access rules, filtration method, or equal share for poor neighborhoods.

Late-eighteenth-century correspondence famously sends ten crates of Kabul grapes as a gift. That is splendid evidence for elite travel, seasonality, packaging, and patronage, but a terrible universal menu. Most people did not breakfast from ten grape crates; grain, pulses, dairy, fruit, and meat varied by household, income, season, faith, and availability.

No reviewed source securely identifies a public hospital, pharmacy register, named physician, vaccination, surgery kit, childbirth manual, or standard household remedy for either target interval. People certainly treated pain, fever, wounds, pregnancy, and infection. The honest card preserves that human certainty without inventing which healer, herb, prayer, or technique they used.

Al-Muqaddasi could praise water and health while criticizing urban cleanliness, but those are comparative traveler judgments, not laboratory tests. No reviewed tenth-century source identifies drains, sewer gradients, cesspits, refuse crews, or a latrine plan. “Healthy water” does not mean microbes politely respected the city limits.

For 1783 to 1800, the reviewed city, manuscript, government, museum, and architectural records still yield no securely dated ordinary toilet. Wells, river access, pots, courtyards, drains, and sweepers performed different tasks; none can be relabeled a sewer by optimism. Later municipal systems cannot be quietly projected backward into Muzaffar Khan’s Multan.

sections.title: Muzaffar Khan inside a Durrani political world

items.text: Timur Shah recovered Multan from the Bhangi Sikhs in 1779 after failed attempts in 1777 and 1778. Muzaffar Khan then ruled locally while acknowledging a Durrani imperial order. Calling him merely an independent king or merely a powerless governor loses the layered sovereignty visible in tribute, fortification, appointment, and war.

The 1783 atlas makes Multan a separate polygon beside Afghanistan, although contemporary politics linked Muzaffar Khan to Durrani authority. That cartographic split may be useful for showing local power, but it cannot settle constitutional status. Maps love crisp borders; eighteenth-century tribute relationships were considerably less cooperative.

Muzaffar Khan’s Multan operated among Durrani court claims, Sikh power, landholding lineages, local officials, messengers, armed retainers, and mobile specialists. Those overlapping relationships reveal politics below the imperial label, but surviving elite records cannot measure every household’s taxes, loyalties, population, or access to a ruler’s court.

Government history credits Muzaffar Khan with thirty-nine years in office before dying in the 1818 defense. Exact starting labels vary among sources, which call him ruler, nawab, or governor. The secure point for this card is continuity beyond 1800: the atlas removes his regime almost two decades too soon.

The 1779 silver issue from Multan marks the last year of the first Sikh occupation and the transition back to Timur Shah. A coin can date authority at the mint more securely than it can map control in every village. Metal changed hands even when tax collectors, landlords, soldiers, and farmers disagreed about who ruled.

sections.title: Shrines, tiles, crafts, and connected art

items.text: Bahauddin Zakariya settled in Multan in the early thirteenth century, and his successors extended a Suhrawardi network across southern Punjab and Sind. His square-and-octagonal mausoleum became part of the city’s enduring sacred geography. Later governors inherited a landscape where pilgrimage, lineage, patronage, markets, and architecture already overlapped.

The tomb of Shah Rukn-e-Alam, built from 1320 to 1324, uses an octagonal mass, tapering brick walls, embedded timber, and glazed decoration. UNESCO treats it as exceptional architecture. The monument’s survival into the Durrani era does not make every repair original; maintaining a centuries-old landmark is itself a continuing human achievement.

A large eighteenth-century molded and glazed earthenware tile attributed to Multan survives at the Metropolitan Museum. Its size and finish show specialized ceramic knowledge. One displaced tile cannot name its kiln workers, wages, building, patron, or route to the market, but it preserves a craft tradition where paperwork often does not.

Multan’s old citadel, mosques, tombs, shops, and walls were not a single ruler’s design. Brickmakers, timber workers, tile makers, calligraphers, plasterers, carriers, water fetchers, cooks, guards, and cleaners kept monumental spaces working. Patrons are named most often because inscriptions and histories liked patrons; buildings quietly remember everybody else.

The city’s achievement was repeated adaptation: a sacred center became an Arab frontier capital, Ismaili principality, sultanate, Mughal province, Durrani governorship, and later Sikh possession without ceasing to be Multan. Continuity belonged to places, communities, skills, and routes more than to any one flag colored over them.

sections.title: Two early endings, and the city keeps going

items.text: The medieval atlas feature ends at 1000, but the Fatimid-aligned principality was not conquered at that software seam. The Institute of Ismaili Studies places Mahmud’s tributary intervention in 1005, followed by further repression. A five-year difference matters when the map pretends a crisp transfer that sources do not synchronize.

At world-1000, the atlas repaints Multan city as “Rajput Kingdoms,” Dera Ghazi Khan as Buyid, and the former target polygon area with other broad features. No reviewed history supports that synchronized rearrangement. It is an editorial mosaic, useful for debugging and unsafe as a literal account of who took each town.

The late atlas feature ends at 1800 by painting Multan and most tested places Sikh. Muzaffar Khan continued to govern until 1818. The 1815 snapshot then paints the same probes Maratha, an even clearer anachronism. Software can move a city twice before history has scheduled the first conquest.

Ranjit Singh’s forces captured Multan in 1818 after repeated earlier attempts. Muzaffar Khan and several sons died in the defense, and the fort and city suffered plunder. The conquest ended his regime and altered taxation and minting; it did not erase residents, shrines, markets, crafts, memories, or the name Multan.

Both overrides therefore leave “fell” null at their atlas endpoints and name no synchronized successor. The card explains the real later transitions while keeping each uncertainty visible. Its shared identity is geographic continuity across discontinuous governments: a city that repeatedly outlived people who were extremely sure their own border color would last forever.

ending.text: This shared card has two separate political endings. The atlas removes its medieval “Multan” feature at 1000, five years before Mahmud of Ghazni made the Ismaili ruler tributary and roughly a decade before renewed conquest and repression. The city itself continues. The atlas then removes “Multan-1783” at 1800 and assigns its core to a Sikh feature, even though Muzaffar Khan remained in power until Ranjit Singh’s 1818 siege; a 1815 snapshot compounds the error by assigning Multan to Maratha. The 1818 conquest killed Muzaffar Khan and sons, damaged and plundered the fort-city, and ended Sadozai rule. It did not end Multan’s households, shrines, bazaars, farms, workshops, languages, or name. Because neither target endpoint matches its documented political defeat, both overrides leave fell null and name no successor at the software seam. One shared card expresses continuity of place and memory across many governments. It does not fuse a tenth-century amirate with an eighteenth-century Durrani province into an impossible nine-hundred-year super-state.
